管風琴主要由木製和金屬材料構成。音管採用錫鉛合金或木材製成，木製音管多用松木或楓: The pipe organ is built mainly of wood and metal. The pipes are made of tin-lead alloy or of wood, the wooden pipes mostly pine or maple. The bellows frame and the keyboard action are made of hardwoods such as oak and beech, which gives the structure its durability. The soundboard and the resonance chamber use spruce or pine. The mechanical drive includes various metal connectors and rods. Leather seals the bellows pallets and the mechanical bearings. Large modern organs also have stop knobs of brass or zinc alloy.
管風琴屬氣鳴樂器，發聲依靠風箱送風吹響音管，每根音管只發一音，音色由該排音管的構: The pipe organ is an aerophone: the bellows deliver air, the air sounds the pipes, and each pipe gives only one note, its timbre fixed by how that rank is built. The player selects ranks with the stops, using them alone or together, and so changes the timbre and the volume; flue pipes sound close to a flute, while reed pipes can come near a brass or woodwind solo. Its air supply is continuous, so pressing a key sustains the note, unlike the piano or the harpsichord, whose strings sound and at once begin to decay. Its range is extremely wide: pipe length sets the pitch, long pipes for the bass and short pipes for the treble, and it can sound harmony in several parts at once.

The pipe organ is a keyboard aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.222.11+421.222.3+412.1, associated with Europe and Greece. A blowing mechanism drives pressurised air into the pipes, the player chooses the notes on the manual and pedal keyboards, and the stops control the timbre, volume and construction of the different ranks. When a key is pressed the corresponding pallet opens and the airflow sounds the pipe; as long as the key is held the note continues. It is common in churches, meeting halls, concert halls, schools and public buildings, and it is used for classical, sacred, secular and popular music.
管風琴為氣鳴鍵盤樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號421.222.11+: The pipe organ is a keyboard aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.222.11+421.222.3+412.1, which originated in ancient Greece and developed in Europe. It is found in churches, meeting halls, concert halls, schools, mansions, public buildings and private houses, and it is used for classical, sacred, secular and popular music. In the silent-film era it accompanied films in the cinema, and municipal auditoriums played orchestral transcriptions on it; in medieval Europe most small-town churches had an organ, and the great cathedrals kept organists.
管風琴起源可追溯至古希臘水壓風琴，約西元前3世紀由亞歷山卓工程師克特西比烏斯創製: The organ can be traced back to the water organ of ancient Greece, built around the 3rd century BC by the Alexandrian engineer Ctesibius, which was blown by water pressure. In the 6th or 7th century bellows replaced the water, and Byzantium kept the instrument; in 757 Constantine V gave one to the Frankish king Pepin the Short, and in 812 Charlemagne sought a similar instrument for the chapel at Aachen, which settled the organ's place in western church music. In the 10th century Winchester Cathedral is recorded as having a large organ. After the 12th century the tone colours grew more complex, and in the 17th century most of the modern classical colours took shape. Before the 18th century organs were mostly designed and built for one church at a time; in the 19th century Cavaillé-Coll pushed factory production, and in the 20th century new organs could imitate different instruments by means of their stops.
